production.text: The launch depended on organized scientific and technical work in a state competition.

evidence.text: Contemporary American responses provide one situated reception of the launch.

name: Sputnik: a signal heard around a divided world
place: Launched from Soviet Central Asia, present-day Kazakhstan
geographicPrecision: Baikonur launch-region locator; no exact trajectory or ground track is reconstructed.

interval.label: Sputnik 1 launched 4 October 1957
interval.note: Launch date, not the whole satellite lifetime, Cold War or history of spaceflight.

question: Why can a scientific achievement also become a political event?
summary: Sputnik 1’s radio signal joined spacecraft, ground observers and competing institutions. Soviet planners simplified a delayed scientific project, then organized a launch that also drew political attention. A translated proposal, technical history and British parliamentary debate show different kinds of work and interpretation around the exact 1957 event.

sections.title: A signal depended on work on Earth
sections.text: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union placed Sputnik 1 in orbit. Its radio transmission could be monitored from the ground. Making that signal possible required more than assembling a sphere: people had to supply power, build transmitters, calculate motion and check whether a launch had achieved an orbit. Scientific observation and state competition shared parts of this infrastructure. NASA places the launch within the International Geophysical Year, whose coordinated investigations gave scientists a timetable extending through 1958.

sections.title: Simplifying the spacecraft changed the organization
sections.text: Historian Asif Siddiqi distinguishes the delayed, more elaborate Object D scientific satellite from the simpler PS-1 that became Sputnik 1. The smaller project concentrated manufacture in Korolev’s design bureau while specialist organizations supplied batteries and radio transmitters. Simplification changed the tasks and dependencies; it did not remove them. A component had to work with other components, and tests had to connect the spacecraft with ground equipment. This is a history of coordinated technical choices rather than a single inventor acting alone.

sections.title: The Soviet proposal made a request, not a result
sections.text: In the 5 January 1957 proposal, Korolev sought permission for launches in April–June. The credited English translation asks for ministries and scientists to cooperate, a coordination commission and equipment for radio and optical tracking. Those requests reveal what planners wanted organized. October’s actual launch also reveals that the hoped-for schedule was not the outcome. A separately catalogued TASS announcement appeared in Pravda on 5 October. GARF’s later project notice quotes its claim to benefit world science and culture. That is a public claim of significance, separate from evidence of the launch or its benefits.

sections.title: Observers argued about what the achievement meant
sections.text: The 29 October Commons debate supplies a response outside the US archive. Questions about Britain falling behind met a reply emphasizing observations for the IGY, including radio astronomy. The Prime Minister distinguished the satellite from the strategic possibilities of its carrier rocket. A scientific observation, an argument about resources and a security concern could therefore surround the same event. These speakers do not stand for everyone in Britain, the Soviet Union or elsewhere. Their differences give us a way to investigate political meaning without assuming one worldwide reaction or an automatic improvement in everyday life.

claims.text: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957.
claims.checkedBy: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval

returnPrompt: What evidence would you need before saying a new technology made life better for everyone?

deeperReading.title: Follow the work beyond the visible object
deeperReading.text: The sphere attracts attention, but the records distribute the work among component producers, coordinating bodies and observers. The proposal treats tracking equipment as part of preparing the project, rather than an optional response after launch. Hansard then records the Prime Minister describing British observation work on both the satellite and its accompanying rocket. Keeping these objects distinct matters: a sighting or tracking claim needs an identified target. The debate can establish what an official reported, while an observing log would be needed to check a particular instrument’s detection.

deeperReading.title: Read each source at its own date and for its purpose
deeperReading.text: The January request aimed to obtain authority and resources before the launch. Its foreign-intelligence claims are not automatically correct: Siddiqi identifies the supposed 1956 US satellite attempt as erroneous. The later historical essay uses records and memoirs that became available after the event; this account does not turn its reconstructed dialogue into a newly heard 1957 recording. The Russian catalogue identifies a 5 October newspaper publication, while GARF’s dated 2017 notice is an anniversary interpretation. Their relationship helps explain how evidence travels through translation, cataloguing and commemoration. It does not merge all these stages into one original artifact. A fuller account needs workers’ records, Soviet and other publics’ varied responses, and the broader institutions of the Cold War; the selected 1955–1958 frame leaves those tasks visible.

evidenceReading.title: Request, announcement and parliamentary response
evidenceReading.introduction: The supplied English account distinguishes a translated planning document, archive metadata and a parliamentary transcription. No original Soviet broadcast, complete newspaper scan or worker interview has been newly inspected.

items.label: A proposal has an intended future
items.text: Korolev’s 5 January request names April–June launches and coordination/tracking tasks. The actual launch date is 4 October.
items.interpretation: The mismatch lets us distinguish an intended schedule from a completed event. The request supplies organizational aims, not proof that every proposed arrangement worked as written.

items.label: An announcement also claims significance
items.text: The Russian catalogue identifies a TASS announcement in Pravda on 5 October. GARF’s 2017 notice quotes its claim of a contribution to world science and culture.
items.interpretation: The catalogue dates a publication and the notice supplies attributed rhetoric. Neither proves equal worldwide benefit or replaces inspection of the complete 1957 newspaper page.

items.label: The debate contains more than one question
items.text: Commons questions concern national priorities and observation. The reply separates scientific tracking from the carrier rocket’s potential strategic effect.
items.interpretation: These are named institutional positions in a dated exchange, not a poll of British people or evidence that every visible object was the satellite itself.

familyActivity.title: Sort a plan, an event and an interpretation
steps: Read the supplied source capsule and make three headings: proposed work, completed event and response.
Place the January request, October launch and Commons exchange under the headings. Compare the hoped-for date with the actual one.
Name one job or coordination task. Explain why completing a spacecraft also required work on the ground.
Write one supported sentence and one further question about who benefited. Do not invent a technician’s words or claim everyone reacted alike.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: On 5 January 1957 Korolev requested permission for simpler satellite launches in April–June and asked for ministries, scientists and tracking equipment to be coordinated. Sputnik 1 launched on 4 October. A Commons debate on 29 October asked about Britain’s priorities and described work observing the satellite and its carrier rocket. These are paraphrases of a credited English translation, NASA’s chronology and a parliamentary transcription. The January request does not certify that its schedule was met; the debate is not everyone’s opinion. This text supplies the dates and tasks needed; no absent photograph, sound recording or historical role-play is required.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian, Soviet/Russian-community or family acceptance
review.scope: Organized technical work, a credited translated Soviet proposal, Russian institutional publication metadata/commemoration and one non-US parliamentary reception. Five new selected source records and two precisely retained-and-renewed catalogue/overview scopes. Original exact 1957 interval/label/note/precision, claims, dimensions, identity, terms and empty object list preserved. No new image, route, map, relation or universal reception claim.
limitations: The registry’s 1945–1991 Cold War reference remains open. This selected 1955–1958 frame is a bounded implementation proposal, not coverage of the entire Cold War, all scientific institutions or every Soviet republic’s experience.

NASA hosts Siddiqi’s credited English edited translation. The original Russian proposal and cited archival records were not independently collated. Incorrect intelligence about a supposed 1956 US satellite attempt is not adopted as US history.

Direct Russian institutional consultation comprises the EBID catalogue and GARF’s 2017 notice. The Pravda scan cache-missed, Rosarkhiv pages timed out and RGANTD returned 502. No complete 1957 announcement, original broadcast/audio, technical drawing or 192-document project inspection is claimed.

The Eisenhower Library statement is retained as catalogue-level consultation. Its one-page PDF exposed no usable body/pixels in this route; no fresh National Science Board quotation or signature reading is supplied.

Hansard records particular questions and official replies, not all British people’s responses or independently checked observing logs. Christchurch library access presented robot verification; newspaper search snippets are not adopted as full articles.

The dossier has no existing media and none is added. NASA’s replica caption does not date a photograph or establish an original-flight image. TASS’s 2017 simulated broadcast is not a 1957 recording. No rights-cleared new image, audio or diagram is promised.

Workers’ conditions, varied Soviet/Kazakh and other publics’ responses and broader postwar institutions need further source work. Independent historical/community review, family usability, screen-reader/device behavior and physical printing remain open.
